title: You Said “I Do”… So Why Do You Still Want Them?
paragraphs:
You Said “I Do”… So Why Do You Still Want Them?
The Quiet Battle No One Talks About in Marriage… and the Grace That Still Chases You
It doesn’t start loud.
It never does.

It’s a glance that lingers just a second too long.
A conversation that feels… easier than it should.
A thought you didn’t invite… but didn’t exactly fight either.

And suddenly you’re sitting there, married… committed… wearing a ring that once felt like fire on your finger…
wondering why your heart is wandering where your body never promised to go.
No one prepared you for this part.

No one told you that you could love your spouse… and still feel temptation toward someone else.
No one warned you that desire doesn’t die at the altar—it just gets redirected… or neglected.
And now you’re asking the question you’re too ashamed to say out loud:
“What’s wrong with me?”
Let this hit you gently… but truthfully:
Nothing is “wrong” with you… but something is at war inside you.
The Apostle Paul didn’t hide this tension. He exposed it brutally:

“For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate…”
(Romans 7:15)

In the original Greek, he says:
“ὃ γὰρ κατεργάζομαι οὐ γινώσκω” (ho gar katergazomai ou ginōskō)
—“What I am working out in my life… I don’t even fully understand.”
You feel that?

Because this isn’t just about attraction.
This is about the battlefield of the heart.
James doesn’t sugarcoat it either:

“But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire.”
(James 1:14)
The Greek word used there is “ἐπιθυμία” (epithymia) — a deep, overreaching desire… not always sinful at its root… but dangerous when it goes ungoverned.
So let’s be honest for a moment.

You didn’t wake up one day and decide to betray your marriage.
But maybe… just maybe… you stopped guarding it.

Maybe you got comfortable.
Maybe the conversations got shallow.
Maybe the intimacy faded into routine.
Maybe the appreciation dried up.
And in that quiet dryness… something else started to feel like rain.
That’s how the enemy works.
Not always through destruction… but through substitution.
Not always through obvious sin… but through emotional drift.
Jesus didn’t ignore this either. He went deeper than behavior… straight to the root:

“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’
But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
(Matthew 5:27–28)
The Greek phrase “πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι” (pros to epithymēsai) means “to deliberately desire… to cultivate longing.”
This isn’t about accidental attraction.
This is about what you choose to feed.

Because attraction may knock…
but lust is when you open the door, pull up a chair, and serve it dinner.
Let this sit with you:

You are not condemned for being tempted.
But you are responsible for what you do with that temptation.
Even Jesus was tempted.

“In every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin.”
(Hebrews 4:15)
The difference?
He didn’t entertain what He refused to become.
So what now?

Do you suppress it?
Ignore it?
Pretend it’s not there?
No.
You bring it into the light before it destroys you in the dark.
The Hebrew word for truth is “אֱמֶת” (emet) — meaning firmness, faithfulness, reality.
Real healing starts with real honesty.

Not polished prayers.
Not religious performance.
But raw confession.

“Search me, O God, and know my heart… test me and know my anxious thoughts.”
(Psalm 139:23)
Because what you refuse to confront… you will eventually become controlled by.
But here’s the part no one tells you:
This struggle doesn’t disqualify you from love… it reveals your need for deeper transformation.
Marriage was never meant to replace your need for Christ.
Your spouse can’t carry what only Jesus was designed to hold.

If you’re looking for someone else to complete what only God can restore…
you’ll keep chasing shadows.
And shadows never satisfy.
So maybe this isn’t just about temptation.
Maybe this is about disconnection… from God first.
Because when your soul starts starving… it will reach for anything that feels like food.
Even if it poisons you slowly.
Jesus said:

“I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger…”
(John 6:35)

Not your coworker.
Not that person in your DMs.
Not the one who “understands you better.”
Only Him.
And here’s the scandal no one expects:
Even if you’ve already entertained it… even if you’ve crossed lines emotionally… even if your thoughts have gone further than you admit…
Grace is still reaching for you.
Right now.

Not after you fix yourself.
Not after you clean it up.
Now.

“Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.”
(Romans 5:20)

The Greek says: “ὑπερεπερίσσευσεν ἡ χάρις” (hyper eperisseusen hē charis)
—Grace didn’t just match your failure… it overflowed beyond it.
So you’re not stuck.
You’re being invited back.

Back to integrity.
Back to truth.
Back to the kind of love that doesn’t wander because it’s rooted.
But this is where you decide:

Will you keep feeding what’s pulling you away…
or start fighting for what you once vowed to protect?
Because love isn’t just a feeling you fell into.
It’s a covenant you fight to keep.
Sit in it.
Be honest.
Someone reading your honesty might finally feel less alone.
And if you want to go deeper—if you’re serious about honoring God not just publicly but privately—stay close.
If this message mattered to you… supporting it helps it reach someone who might be one decision away from breaking something sacred.

Because glorifying God isn’t just about what you believe…
it’s also about what you help spread.
And here’s the truth that won’t leave you:
Temptation may knock on your door… but grace is still standing inside your house, asking you who you really belong to.
